note: Scores for the three governance scales. Options a card can choose (decision approaches, joining tiers and ways, conflict approaches) are scored on what they are (joining options only on Transparent and Hierarchical, from the members' point of view; conflict approaches' Participatory is how much the community takes part, agreed 2026-10-09): a card's score on a scale is the average of the accepted scores of what it chose (rounded to a whole number, on the same 1–7 range). Values (list "values") are scored on where they point: a community that holds the value would tend to want that end; they suggest values from a card's target scales (basics.targetScales). null = says nothing about that scale: left out of a card's average; for suggestions, it counts as neutralDistance (an average fit, neither close nor far). Each scale's levels: what each score means, from range.min to range.max (1, 4 and 7 are the anchors the scores were drafted against). Each scale's ends: the trade-offs of being at the low (1) or high (7) end (pros: what you gain; cons: what it costs), short phrases, with an optional short title where the level's own text is too long for the box, shown when a community chooses its targets. Only status "accepted" is used ("proposed" = drafted, waiting for the team's review). Reviewed in the workbench, bench.html. How each scale applies to each kind of option is in each scale's "applies" (decision, conflict, joining, values). An option that says nothing about a scale is null ("—") and is left out of a card's average, not counted as low. The scales describe; they don't judge.

scales.label: Participatory
scales.description: How many members take part in a decision, and how much say they have.
levels: One person, or a few, decide
A small group decides, sometimes asking others
A few decide, after hearing from members
A share of the members take part, or have some say
Most members can have a say; a smaller group decides
Nearly everyone takes part in most decisions
Everyone takes part

applies.decision: How many members take part in making decisions, and how much say they have (1: one person or a few decide; 7: everyone takes part, as in consensus; votes are 6: everyone has a say, but only through a ballot).
applies.conflict: How much of the community takes part in resolving a conflict, beyond the people in it (a community vote 6; circles and restorative practices 5; mediation by one neutral person 3; a manager deciding 1).
applies.joining: Not scored: how open joining is shows in the joining tiers themselves (open, tiered, approvals, closed).
applies.values: Where a community that holds the value would tend to want to be.

scales.label: Transparent
scales.description: How visible the process, the criteria and the reasons are to members (not necessarily to the public).
levels: Private: decisions and reasons aren't seen
Some outcomes are shared, rarely the reasons
Outcomes are shared; the reasons only if asked
Outcomes are visible; the reasons and process not always
Outcomes and reasons are shared; the discussion isn't
The process and reasons are mostly open, and recorded
Fully open: the process, discussion and reasons are recorded for all

applies.decision: Whether the discussion, the reasons and the outcome are visible and recorded.
applies.conflict: Whether the process and outcome are visible. Confidential processes (mediation, circles, restorative practices) score low by design; that isn't a flaw.
applies.joining: Whether the criteria for joining, and decisions about who joins, are visible.
applies.values: Where a community that holds the value would tend to want to be.

scales.label: Hierarchical
scales.description: How much the authority to decide sits with particular people, roles or levels, rather than with members as equals.
levels: Flat: no role carries more authority
Nearly flat: some roles coordinate, but don't decide
A few roles carry a little more weight
Some roles carry more weight
Clear roles, some with authority over others
Several levels, with most authority near the top
Clear levels, with authority at the top

applies.decision: Who decides: members as equals (1), roles that coordinate but don't decide (2), roles with more weight (3–4), roles with authority over others (5), a leader or the top of several levels (6–7).
applies.conflict: Who decides the outcome: the people involved, as equals (1–2), a council or panel of members (3–4), an arbitrator, manager or other single role (5–7).
applies.joining: Who holds the gate, from the members' point of view: all members together (1), some members (3), a gatekeeper, or levels of membership (5).
applies.values: Where a community that holds the value would tend to want to be.

items.why: Anyone can object, proposals are shared openly for a set time, and no role holds a veto.
Whoever takes on the work decides, so anyone can take part by acting, though decisions aren't always discussed first.
Everyone must agree, which means everyone takes part, usually in open discussion, with no one deciding alone.
Authority sits with one person or group at a time, but everyone takes a turn.
Everyone works towards agreement in the open, with a vote as the fallback.
Members give input, but delegates shape the final decision.
Decisions are made by consent in small circles, linked by roles, with records shared between circles.
Every member votes, and a large majority is needed, so no group can decide alone.
Every member votes; results are counted openly, though reasons aren't part of the vote.
Every member scores the options; results are counted openly, though reasons aren't part of the vote.
Every member votes and the majority decides; results are open, though reasons aren't part of the vote.
Every member votes for each option they accept; results are open, though reasons aren't part of the vote.
Members vote, but some members' votes count for more, by seniority or contribution.
Every member votes and can show how strongly they feel; no role counts for more.
Every member votes and can show how strongly they feel, at a rising cost; no role counts for more.
Every member can vote and change their vote over time, with the running tally visible.
Members discuss and decide together on a shared tool, where the discussion and the outcome are recorded for all to see.
A random, representative sample of members deliberates in small groups, hearing different views, and is polled before and after.
A board, with seats given to investors or stakeholders, makes the key decisions.
Members choose the board, but the board makes the decisions.

One leader decides alone, without the group's input.

Anyone can join, with little or no gatekeeping.

Joining needs approval, from existing members or a gatekeeping process.

An onboarding team reviews applications.

The group interviews newcomers together.
Joining needs passing an assessment or a portfolio review.
Members are chosen at random from those eligible, so no one holds the gate, though few get in each time.
Trained members help their peers resolve disputes, usually in private.
Senior members guide or decide disputes.
A neutral facilitator helps the parties negotiate.
Arbitrators chosen for each case, often from within the community, decide it.
The people involved work through the dispute together in structured sessions.
Members vote to resolve the dispute, and a large majority is needed.
The parties look for a solution that meets everyone's underlying interests.
Those involved and affected talk through the harm and how to repair it, usually in confidence.

Those involved and affected take part in a structured dialogue with equal input, usually in confidence.
A standing committee judges disputes.
A manager or leader makes a binding decision.
A formal hearing body within the community decides.
Everyone works together towards a resolution they can all agree to.

An arbitrator recommends a resolution that the parties can accept or not.

Members chosen at random resolve the dispute or form the jury.
Members take turns handling disputes.
